facts: The Dolomites are a mountain range located in northeastern Italy, famous for their distinctive jagged pale limestone peaks.
Formed millions of years ago from fossilized coral reefs, these mountains were designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2009.
The highest peak in the Dolomites is Marmolada, standing proudly at over three thousand three hundred meters tall.
During sunrise and sunset, the rocky peaks glow in shades of pink and orange, a phenomenon called enrosadira.
Legendary cyclist Fausto Coppi conquered many famous steep mountain passes here during the historic Giro d'Italia races.
The famous Lavaredo Ultra Trail attracts elite trail runners from all over the world to these breathtaking alpine paths.
Local mountain cuisine blends Italian classics with Austrian flavors, featuring hearty dumplings called casunziei and apple strudel.
Ancient Ladin language and culture are still passionately preserved by local communities living in the high mountain valleys.
Cortina d'Ampezzo hosted the Winter Olympic Games in 1956 and will co-host them again in 2026.
The famous Tre Cime di Lavaredo are three distinctive rock pillars that form one of Europe's most iconic landscapes.
Hundreds of miles of climbing paths called via ferrata were originally built in these mountains during World War One.
Mountain goats called chamois and agile alpine ibex can often be spotted scaling the steep rocky slopes.
Beautiful Lake Braies is world-famous for its crystal turquoise waters reflecting dramatic surrounding limestone cliffs.
The Alta Via 1 trail stretches over one hundred kilometers, offering one of Europe's premier multi-day mountain trekking routes.
World-famous mountaineer Reinhold Messner, who climbed all fourteen eight-thousand-meter peaks, was born and raised in this region.
Vibrant alpine meadows across the range blossom with protected wildflower species like edelweiss throughout the warm summer months.
